name: Farmer's Carry
tierNote: Safety tier A (content.md appendix B); census.json difficulty tier 3.

claims.text: Dumbbells, kettlebells, a trap bar or farmer's handles can be used; one source says the base mechanics are the same whichever tool is used.

quotes.text: You can use various tools to perform farmer’s carries with — two barbells loaded with weight plates, farmer’s carry handles, dumbbells or kettlebells. Even a trap bar is a suitable carrying implement. Whichever tool you choose, the base mechanics are the same.
quotes.where: How to Do the Farmer’s Carry, Equipment Needed

quotes.text: You can use kettlebells, dumbbells, a trap bar, or dedicated Farmer’s Walk handles.
quotes.where: Opening paragraphs, under the page subtitle 'Learn how to do this full-body exercise and improve many aspects of your fitness'

claims.text: Clear a level, dry route first, with room to turn and a clear place to set the weights down, away from the feet and other people.

quotes.text: Clear a level, dry route before picking up the weights. Leave space to turn and a clear area to set them down, away from your feet and other people.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk (below the in-page 'Get Fitter, Faster' promo heading)

claims.text: Stand between the weights, feet about hip-width apart; bend at the hips and knees, take a secure neutral grip, brace and stand up with the legs, without jerking the handles.

quotes.text: Stand between the weights with your feet about hip-width apart. Bend at your hips and knees, take a secure grip, brace your trunk, and stand up without jerking the handles.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk (below the in-page 'Get Fitter, Faster' promo heading)

quotes.text: Hinge at your hips to bend over and grab each dumbbell. Lift with your legs to stand up with the weights.
quotes.where: How to Do the Farmer’s Carry, Step 1

quotes.text: Reach down to grip the handles using a neutral grip, then deadlift the weights to your sides.
quotes.where: How to Do the Farmer’s Carry

claims.text: Start and walk with the arms fully extended (long) at the sides, a tall chest, a braced core, the shoulder blades pinched, the neck and spine neutral, the torso upright and the gaze ahead.

quotes.text: In your starting position, you should have your arms fully extended at your sides, a tall chest, braced core, pinched shoulder blades, and a neutral neck and spine.
quotes.where: How to Do the Farmer’s Carry

quotes.text: Keep your arms long, your torso upright, and your gaze ahead. Walk with controlled steps.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk (below the in-page 'Get Fitter, Faster' promo heading)

claims.text: Many lifters may shrug their shoulders high to make up for fatigue; keep the shoulders back and down, without forcing a shrug or an exaggerated shoulders-back position.

quotes.text: Many lifters may try to compensate for fatigue by shrugging their shoulders high. And while that’s good when you’re trying to perform shrugs, you want to try to keep your shoulders back and down during farmer’s carries to maximize your upper back activation.
quotes.where: Common Farmer’s Carry Mistakes: Poor Upper Back Positioning

quotes.text: Avoid forcing your shoulders into a shrug or an exaggerated shoulders-back position.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk (below the in-page 'Get Fitter, Faster' promo heading)

claims.text: Check that the neck is not scrunched, the shoulders not rounded forward, the back not arched and the knees not locked out; one source says these usually mean the load is too heavy.

quotes.text: Mentally check that you’re not scrunching your neck, rounding your shoulders forward, arching your back, or locking out your knees while performing your farmer’s carry
quotes.where: Common Farmer’s Carry Mistakes: Tensing All the Wrong Places

quotes.text: These characteristics usually indicate that you’re struggling to carry a load that’s too heavy for you.
quotes.where: Common Farmer’s Carry Mistakes: Tensing All the Wrong Places

claims.text: Rushing is risky: a single misstep could pull a calf muscle, roll an ankle or twist a knee. Going slow keeps the form strong and the posture tight; do not speed up to get more distance.

quotes.text: Rushing through the movement is a recipe for disaster, as a single misstep could be the reason you pull your calf muscle, roll your ankle, twist your knee, or experience any of many injuries
quotes.where: Trainer Tips for Form: Stay Slow and Steady

quotes.text: Going slow is the best way to keep your form strong and posture tight.
quotes.where: Trainer Tips for Form: Stay Slow and Steady

quotes.text: Do not speed up to squeeze out more distance.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk, Important tips

claims.text: Take short steps: one source says short, deliberate steps; another short, fast strides; a third starts with small steps and lengthens the stride as speed rises.

quotes.text: Start walking in a straight line, taking short, deliberate steps.
quotes.where: How to Do the Farmer’s Carry

quotes.text: Use short, fast strides to increase your performance.
quotes.where: How to Do the Farmer’s Carry, Step 2

quotes.text: Look ahead, and start moving forward in small steps. Increase the stride length as you increase the speed.
quotes.where: How to Do Farmers Walk, step 4

claims.text: Stay steady and upright, with the body in a straight line; don't lean excessively forward, and don't let the weight move sideways or favour one side.

quotes.text: Maintain a steady, upright position and posture. Do not allow the weight to move laterally or favor one side over the other.
quotes.where: How to Do the Farmer’s Carry, Step 2

quotes.text: Try to keep your body in a straight line and not lean excessively forward as you walk.
quotes.where: How to Do Farmers Walk, step 5

quotes.text: You should be able to lift the weights, walk without leaning or stumbling, and lower them under control.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk (below the in-page 'Get Fitter, Faster' promo heading)

claims.text: Not bracing the core can wreak havoc on the lower back; to brace, take a deep breath in, then exhale and tighten the abdominal muscles.

quotes.text: The farmer’s walk exercise can wreak havoc on your lower back if you’re not bracing your core.
quotes.where: Trainer Tips for Form: Brace Your Core

quotes.text: Take a deep breath in, letting your rib cage expand, then exhale, contract your abdominal muscles, and draw the belly button towards your spine
quotes.where: Trainer Tips for Form: Brace Your Core

claims.text: Breathe in and grip the handles, then hold the breath, brace slightly and lift the weights.

quotes.text: Inhale, lean forward and grip the handles.
quotes.where: How to Do Farmers Walk, step 2

quotes.text: Hold your breath, brace your core slightly, and lift the weights.
quotes.where: How to Do Farmers Walk, step 3

claims.text: Said of the strongman-style carry with farmer's handles: once walking, don't forget to breathe.

quotes.text: Begin walking. Don’t forget to breathe.
quotes.where: Farmer’s Carry Variations and Alternatives: Strongman-Style Farmer’s Carry

claims.text: Grip with the bottom of the palm pushed into the handle, not with the fingers alone; curl the hand and fingers around it, wrap the thumb and squeeze hard.

quotes.text: Instead of gripping the handle of your kettlebell or dumbbell with your fingers, reach all the way down until the bottom of your palm is pushed into the handle
quotes.where: Trainer Tips for Form: Get a Good Grip

quotes.text: Then, curl your hand and fingers around the handle, wrap your thumb, and squeeze hard.
quotes.where: Trainer Tips for Form: Get a Good Grip

claims.text: Without a good grip the weights may slip, land on the toe or bounce into the ankle.

quotes.text: Without a good grip, the weights may slip from your grasp, land on your toe, bounce into your ankle, or cause some other catastrophic series of unfortunate events.
quotes.where: Trainer Tips for Form: Get a Good Grip

claims.text: Stop before the grip fails: if a handle starts slipping, the posture changes or the steps lose control, end the carry. Stop if you feel pain.

quotes.text: Stop before your grip fails. If a handle starts slipping, your posture changes, or you lose control of your steps, end the carry. Do not speed up to squeeze out more distance. Stop if you feel pain.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk, Important tips

claims.text: Set-down: come to a stable stop while still in control, keep the weights beside you, bend at the hips and knees and lower them to the floor with the feet clear, holding on until they are supported and not turning while lowering.

quotes.text: Come to a stable stop while you still control the weights. Keep them beside you, bend at your hips and knees, and lower them to the floor with your feet clear. Keep hold until the implements are supported; avoid turning while lowering them.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk, Important tips: Plan the set-down

quotes.text: When you are done, lower the implements back to the ground in a controlled manner.
quotes.where: How to Do Farmers Walk, step 6

claims.text: Slow before a turn and change direction with several small steps, feet and torso together, not a sharp pivot on planted feet; if space is tight, set the weights down first.

quotes.text: Slow before a turn and change direction with several small steps, moving your feet and torso together. Avoid a sharp pivot with your feet planted. If space is tight, finish the carry and set the weights down before repositioning.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk (below the in-page 'Get Fitter, Faster' promo heading)

claims.text: Load progression: start with a manageable load and a short route, about 25% of body weight in each hand for a beginner; repeat it until the pickup, walk, turns and set-down stay controlled, then add a little load or distance, not both, and scale gradually.

quotes.text: Start with a manageable load and a short route.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk (below the in-page 'Get Fitter, Faster' promo heading)

quotes.text: Repeat a manageable load until the pickup, walk, turns, and set-down stay controlled. Then consider a small increase in load or distance, rather than changing both at once.
quotes.where: How To Do The Farmer’s Walk, Important tips

quotes.text: Dumbbells that are approximately 25% of your body weight in each hand are a great place to start
quotes.where: Common Farmer’s Carry Mistakes: Choosing the Wrong Weight

quotes.text: You may progress to lifting 50%, 75%, or even 100% of your body weight later on, but make sure you scale gradually.
quotes.where: Common Farmer’s Carry Mistakes: Choosing the Wrong Weight

claims.text: The forearm (finger) flexors work to hold the handles, and grip can limit the carry before the legs tire.

quotes.text: Forearms – the finger flexors in your forearms work to hold the handles. Grip demands can limit the carry before your legs tire.

quotes.text: This large muscle plays a vital role in stabilizing the scapula (shoulder blades) as it is the main muscle producing tension in the upper back while holding the weight in your hands.

claims.text: The glutes and obliques work too: one source lists both as primary muscles, and another says the carry strengthens the gluteus medius, which steadies the torso and pelvis.

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; the tall, upright torso with the arms long at the sides (c4, c9), the shoulders back and down and the plate fault, steps too long (c25), and the short steps (c8) read from the side.
plate.equipment: Two dumbbells (census need dumbbell, exists), one in each hand at the sides; floor line (census floor). The trap bar is the listed alternative (variantLine).
plate.start: One step: torso upright, gaze ahead, neck and spine neutral, chest tall (c4); arms fully extended at the sides, a dumbbell in each hand in a neutral grip, thumb wrapped (c3, c4, c13); shoulders back and down, not shrugged (c5); feet about hip-width, one foot starting a short step (c3, c8).
plate.end: The next short step, with the same tall torso, long arms and level weights (c4, c8, c9).

checkpoints.label: Shoulders down
checkpoints.what: Shoulders back and down, not shrugged.

checkpoints.label: Arms long
checkpoints.what: Arms fully extended at your sides.

mistake.what: Steps too long for a beginner.
mistake.why: The top fault, rushing (c7), is speed only, so the plate draws the next fault: BarBend's list, the anchor's, names stride length after a load choice (c25), and two sources say short steps (c8).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: rushing (c7). Reading applied: D-SUP-LB10-MAY (#296, comment 6343484589). Step 1 finds no hit. Set aside: BarBend's "Many lifters may try to compensate for fatigue by shrugging their shoulders high." ('may', D-SUP-LB10-MAY); Garage Gym Reviews' "These characteristics usually indicate that you’re struggling to carry a load that’s too heavy for you." (c6) says what the tension faults point to, the load, a cause, not how often they happen (renegade_row, R-LB7); the list headings and intros (BarBend's "Common Farmer’s Carry Mistakes" and "Be sure you’re not falling prey to these common flaws in farmer’s carry training.", Garage Gym Reviews' "Here are some of the most common mistakes associated with the farmer’s carry." and "common mistakes to avoid") are list headings and list sentences; BarBend's "which is usually lacking in beginners" (balance in beginners), "there are often advantages to taking it more accessible" (load), "Strongman competitions typically use special handles", "athletes typically perform heavy carries", "Using a dumbbell will likely be the easiest implement for most beginners", "Use about 60 to 65 percent of your typical weight", "the most notable benefits", "commonly referred to", "most commonly known", "most notably", "many disciplines", "many variations" and "the most beneficial to maximal output"; Garage Gym Reviews' "many farmers have strength", "Sets of farmer’s carries often consist of just one walk", "most lifters can move more weight on a barbell bench press ... trap-bar carries often allow you to carry more weight" and "everyone can benefit"; and the op-ed's "a common strongman event", "most likely causing you to drop" (hand placement on strongman handles, a grip) and "you will most likely feel more comfortable with an even stance" are about implements, loads, muscles, benefits, programming, another exercise or the article, not how often a fault happens. Step 2, named faults (plate.mistake, handlingMistakes or a mistakes list) tied to harm: only rushing, Garage Gym Reviews' "Rushing through the movement is a recipe for disaster, as a single misstep could be the reason you pull your calf muscle, roll your ankle, twist your knee, or experience any of many injuries" (c7); its "take your time on these to reap the most benefit from each carry and minimize your risk of injury" is the same item's advice. Not tied to harm: the shrug (BarBend's "to maximize your upper back activation" and "It will also help prevent you from resting the weights on your sides."); stride length (BarBend's "might throw you off balance", c25); Garage Gym Reviews' tensing item ("may produce adverse effects": no load and no injury, D-SUP-STRAIN); the lean (c9, no harm). Not named faults, so not counted: not bracing (c10 "can wreak havoc on your lower back", and "abdominal bracing stabilizes the spine, which may reduce your risk of injury", a tips section); the op-ed's walking before standing tall, "it will put more strain on your lower back" (c24, WEAK; 'strain' counts under D-SUP-STRAIN, but the fault is a strongman-handle technique on no list and not on the card's faults), and its "the weight can start to swing forward and back" and turning line "to avoid momentum twisting the farmers in front of you causing it impede your steps or even drop the handles" (strongman handles, no harm word); the loose grip (c14, a grip, no LR-31 harm word). Not faults: BarBend's "a large amount of strain is placed on the shoulder joint" (holding a load, muscles section) and "without all that pressure on your elbows" (front-rack variation); BarBend's benefit lines ("the prevention and reduction of low back pain", "aiding in injury prevention", "the protection of the spine", "can help alleviate lower back pain", "protecting the spine"); Garage Gym Reviews' trap-bar "reduce the strain on the lower back" (equipment); load lines ("Struggling to move weights that are too heavy may cause our form to deteriorate, leaving us susceptible to injury", "if you’re dropping the weights left and right", BarBend's "Going Too Light"; LR-31); Fitness Volt's "not a guarantee against injury", "an injury-free load for every reader", "or prevent injury" and "Do not judge a carry by how much discomfort you can tolerate" (disclaimers and programming) and "Stop if you feel pain." (a stop line, c15). Rushing is speed only, so drawable is false and handlingMistakes[0] is rushing. plate.mistake by the same steps: step 1 none, step 2 none left, so step 3. Two lists are written for this exercise (BarBend's, Garage Gym Reviews'); the anchor's comes first (anchorSource bb-farmers). Its item 1, "Going Too Light", is a load choice, not a candidate; item 2, "Stride Length": "Trying to take regular-sized steps as a beginner might throw you off balance." (c25). Steps too long are a still sign the side view shows, so plate.mistake is steps too long for a beginner.

tempo.text: Walk: short steps (c8). The sources differ on speed: Garage Gym Reviews and Fitness Volt walk slowly and with control (c7, c4), BarBend uses short, fast strides, and StrengthLog lengthens the stride as speed rises (c8). No source gives seconds, a step rate or a pause, so no seconds are drawn (LR-33; R-LB2-1).

plate.variantLine: exercises.json lists Dumbbells / Trap Bar. The plate draws dumbbells (census need dumbbell). BarBend says the base mechanics are the same whichever tool is used, trap bar included (c1), so the posture, shoulder, step, bracing, breathing, stop and load claims (c4-c11, c15, c18) hold for both. The neutral dumbbell pickup beside the feet (c3), the palm-in grip (c13) and the set-down with the weights beside you (c16) are written for weights at the sides; the trap bar is deadlifted from inside the frame and carried with the arms fully extended (c23).

grip.type: Neutral grip, one dumbbell handle in each hand at the sides (c3, c4).
grip.width: Hands at the sides of the body (c4).
grip.handContact: Bottom of the palm pushed into the handle, hand and fingers curled around it (c13).
grip.note: No source gives a wrist position; the plate draws the hold hand-pair's straight wrist as a drawing convention (LR-4).

setup.step: Clear a level, dry route, with room to set down.
Stand between the weights, feet about hip-width apart.
Bend at your hips and knees and grip, thumbs wrapped.
Breathe in, brace, and stand up without jerking the weights.
Stand fully tall before your first step.

posture.point: Shoulders back and down, not shrugged.
Weights even, not shifting to one side.
Slow down and turn with small steps.

handlingMistakes.fix: Slow down. Don't speed up for more distance.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Steps too long for your level.
Shrugging your shoulders up as you tire.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep your shoulders back and down.

breathing.text: Breathe in and brace to lift, then keep breathing as you walk.

rows.means: They work to hold the handles.
They hold your shoulder blades steady under the load.

rows.fix: End the carry and set the weights down.
Brace before you lift. Stop if you feel pain.

risks.risk: Rushing is risky: one misstep could pull a calf, roll an ankle or twist a knee.
Not bracing your core can wreak havoc on your lower back.
Without a good grip, the weights may slip and land on your toe.

zooms.right: Palm pushed into the handle, thumb wrapped.

libraryDiff.why: Library: forearms and upper_traps primary; core and glutes secondary. StrengthLog lists the forearm flexors and trapezius as primary (c19, c20), and Fitness Volt and BarBend say they hold the handles and the shoulder blades (c19, c20). StrengthLog also lists glutes and obliques as primary, and BarBend says the carry strengthens the gluteus medius (c21); the card's feel keeps them secondary, as the library does. core goes in no feel role (LR-35), so obliques stand for it in feel; the library's core stays. No change proposed.

loadProgression.text: Start with a manageable load, about a quarter of your body weight in each hand. Repeat it until the whole carry stays controlled. Then consider a little more load or distance, not both.

gaps: Breathing (content.md 5.2): no source read gives the squat's blood-pressure breath-holding line. StrengthLog holds the breath to lift (c11) and BarBend's strongman section says keep breathing (c12, WEAK); the card shows only that. Left out, not invented.
Way out: letting go of the weights in a fall or stumble (dropping them away from the feet) has no source. The sourced way out is ending the carry and the controlled set-down (c15, c16).

wayOut.text: Handle slipping, posture changing or steps out of control? End the carry. Stop while you still control the weights, keep them beside you, bend your hips and knees and lower them, feet clear.

safetyPoints: Way out: end the carry before the grip fails (c15) and the controlled set-down (c16, c2); dropping the weights in a stumble is a gap.
Breathing: c11, c10, c12 (breathing); the blood-pressure line is a gap.
Warning link: feel.rows[3] links the back box (c10, c11, c15); its stop line cites Fitness Volt's "Stop if you feel pain." (R-LB6-6).
Safeties or J-hooks, bar path clear of the neck: not applicable (no bar overhead or in a rack).

notes: Anchor: BarBend's farmer's-carry page (Austin Current), read in full (steps, variations including the trap bar, sets, muscles, common-mistakes list, FAQs). Garage Gym Reviews' farmer's-carry page, Fitness Volt's farmer's-walk page (updated 2026-09-12) and StrengthLog's farmers-walk page were read in full too.

bb-fwbreak is a BarBend op-ed written for strongman farmer's handles, another implement: its one claim (c24) is WEAK and says so. Its handle-placement and turning lines are implement-specific and not used.
StrengthLog's steps are written for 'farmers walk-cases, or similar implements'; its lines used here (breath, small steps, straight line, set-down) are not implement-specific.

Shared cards: none lists lib_farmer_s_carry in appliesTo (shared/ at the start head). The lower-back row links redFlag 'back' as a pending link (LR-11, LR-27, LR-28): the sheet cannot ship before the back-pain box, and back-pain-box.json's appliesTo does not yet list this id.

Shoulders: BarBend says keep the shoulders back and down, Garage Gym Reviews pinches the shoulder blades (c4), and Fitness Volt warns against forcing a shrug or an exaggerated shoulders-back position (c5). The card says back and down, without forcing.
Speed: Garage Gym Reviews and Fitness Volt say slow and controlled, BarBend short, fast strides (c7, c8). The shown lines say short, deliberate steps and the rushing fault, from the slow line.

Read but not cited: McGill 2009 (PubMed 19528856, abstract, efetch; Fitness Volt's source [2]): strongman events and spine load, nothing farmer's-walk specific in the abstract. 404 or 502 on 2026-10-22: healthline.com farmers-walk, puregym.com farmers-walk, muscleandfitness.com farmers-walk (502); ACE farmer's-carry URL redirects to the library index.
